subject: Physics
title: Electromagnetic Induction
summary: A changing magnetic flux produces an emf. That single idea, discovered by Faraday and Henry, gives us Faraday's law, Lenz's law, motional emf, self and mutual inductance and the AC generator. The chapter is short, its derivations are fixed and predictable, and it pairs with Alternating Current to form Unit IV of the board paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit IV (Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents, Chapters 6 and 7) carries 8 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. This chapter typically contributes 3 to 5 of those marks: usually one derivation (motional emf, rotating rod, self or mutual inductance, or the AC generator) as a 3- or 5-mark question, plus one or two 1-mark questions on Lenz's law or flux.

question_types.note: Rate of change of flux from a given Φ(t), direction of induced current from Lenz's law, how self-inductance changes when turns or length change, the SI unit of flux or inductance, and the orientation of the coil in an AC generator when the emf is maximum.

Lenz's law and conservation of energy, self-inductance as the inertia of electricity, whether inductance depends on current, a rod moving parallel to the field, and a copper ring jumping off a solenoid.

State Lenz's law or Faraday's law, define self or mutual inductance with the SI unit, give the direction of induced current in a described situation, or a one-step numerical on ε = −dΦ/dt or ε = L dI/dt.

Derive the emf across a rotating rod, ε = ½Bωl<sup>2</sup>; derive the energy stored in an inductor; a motional-emf numerical with current, force and power; explain why a rectangular loop leaving a field gives a constant emf while a circular one does not.

Define mutual inductance and derive M = μ<sub>0</sub>n<sub>1</sub>n<sub>2</sub>πr<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>l for coaxial solenoids; derive L = μ<sub>0</sub>n<sup>2</sup>Al for a solenoid; derive motional emf from the Lorentz force and show that mechanical power equals Joule heat; the AC generator with a labelled diagram, derivation and graph.
A passage on Faraday's experiments, Lenz's law, the falling magnet in a copper tube, or the AC generator, followed by four short parts including one small numerical.

sections.heading: 6.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Oersted showed in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic field. The natural next question was whether a magnetic field can produce an electric current. Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in the United States answered it around 1830, independently: a steady magnetic field does nothing, but a changing magnetic field, or a conductor moving through a magnetic field, drives a current in a closed circuit. The phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction, the emf produced is the induced emf, and the current it drives is the induced current.

Why the board cares: every generator in every power station, every transformer on the grid, the induction cooktop, the metal detector and the wireless charger run on this one idea. In the paper, the chapter shows up as a chain of derivations that all start from the same line, ε = −dΦB/dt. If you can write that line and know what ΦB is in each situation, you can reproduce everything that follows.

The rationalised NCERT chapter has these sections: Faraday and Henry's experiments, magnetic flux, Faraday's law, Lenz's law and conservation of energy, motional emf, inductance (mutual and self) and the AC generator. The older sections on eddy currents and the quantitative energy treatment of the moving arm were removed from the textbook, though the energy argument still makes a good 3-mark question and is included below.
sections.tip: The examiner wants the word 'change' in your definition. 'A magnetic field produces a current' loses the mark; 'a changing magnetic flux produces an emf' gets it.

sections.heading: 6.2 The Experiments of Faraday and Henry
sections.body:
NCERT describes three experiments. You should be able to describe each in two or three lines and state what it proves.

Experiment 6.1: magnet and coil. A coil C1 is connected to a galvanometer. When the north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards the coil, the galvanometer deflects. When the magnet is held still, there is no deflection. When the magnet is pulled away, the deflection reverses. Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same result, and moving faster gives a larger deflection. Conclusion: relative motion between magnet and coil induces a current, and the current lasts only while the motion lasts.

Experiment 6.2: two coils. The bar magnet is replaced by a second coil C2 carrying a steady current from a battery. Moving C2 towards or away from C1 produces the same deflections as the magnet did. A current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet, so this is the same effect.

Experiment 6.3: no motion at all. Both coils are kept fixed. C2 is connected to a battery through a tapping key. The galvanometer in C1 shows a momentary deflection when the key is pressed and a deflection in the opposite direction when it is released. With the key held pressed, there is nothing. Conclusion: what matters is not motion but a change in the magnetic field through C1. Faraday later found that an iron rod inserted along the axis of the coils makes the deflection much larger.

A classic 2-mark question (NCERT Example 6.1) asks how to get a larger deflection: move the magnet faster, use a stronger magnet, use a coil with more turns or larger area, or insert a soft-iron core. And how to show the induced current without a galvanometer: replace it with a small torch bulb or an LED, which glows briefly.
sections.tip: In the two-coil experiment the deflection on pressing the key is opposite to the deflection on releasing it. Say why: the flux through C<sub>1</sub> increases in one case and decreases in the other.

sections.heading: 6.3 Magnetic Flux
sections.body:
Magnetic flux through a surface measures how much of the field passes through it. For a plane surface of area A placed in a uniform field B, with θ the angle between B and the normal to the surface,

ΦB = B · A = BA cos θ

For a general surface split into small elements dAi, ΦB = ∑ Bi · dAi. Flux is a scalar. Its SI unit is the weber (Wb); 1 Wb = 1 T m2. The tesla itself is 1 Wb m−2, which is why the field is sometimes called flux density.

Three cases to keep straight. When the field is perpendicular to the surface (parallel to the normal), θ = 0 and ΦB = BA, the maximum. When the field lies in the plane of the surface, θ = 90° and ΦB = 0. When the surface is turned through 180°, the flux changes sign, from +BA to −BA, so the change in flux is 2BA. This last point is the whole trick in NCERT Example 6.3 and in the search-coil type numericals.

For a coil of N turns, each turn links the same flux, so the total flux linkage is NΦB. The flux through a coil can change in three ways, and each gives a family of exam questions: B changes with time (a solenoid whose current is changed, a decaying field), the area changes (a loop being pulled out of a field, a loop deformed from a circle into a narrow line), or the angle changes (a coil rotating in a field, which is the generator).

where: angle between B and the normal to the surface
weber, the SI unit of magnetic flux

sections.tip: θ is measured from the normal, not from the plane. A field 'in the north-east direction across a vertical east-west loop' makes 45° with the normal, so Φ = BA cos 45°.

sections.heading: 6.4 Faraday's Law of Induction
sections.body:
Faraday summarised his experiments in one law. The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit. In symbols,

ε = −dΦB/dt

The negative sign is Lenz's law, the direction of the emf, which is the subject of the next section. For a closely wound coil of N turns the flux through each turn changes at the same rate, so the emf is N times larger:

ε = −N dΦB/dt

Because ΦB = BA cos θ, the emf can be produced by changing B, or A, or θ, or any combination. The examiner accepts the law in words or symbols but wants both when the question says 'state'.

Two model numericals. NCERT Example 6.2: a square loop of side 10 cm and resistance 0.5 Ω stands vertically in the east-west plane; a field of 0.10 T pointing north-east is reduced to zero in 0.70 s at a steady rate. The normal to the loop points north, so θ = 45°. Initial flux = 0.10 × (0.10)2 × cos 45° = 7.07 × 10−4 Wb. Emf = 7.07 × 10−4/0.70 = 1.0 × 10−3 V, current = 1.0 × 10−3/0.5 = 2.0 × 10−3 A.

NCERT Example 6.3: a coil of radius 10 cm, 500 turns and resistance 2 Ω has its plane perpendicular to the horizontal component of the earth's field, 3.0 × 10−5 T, and is rotated about a vertical diameter through 180° in 0.25 s. Flux per turn goes from +BA to −BA, so the change is 2BA and the total change in flux linkage is 2NBA = 2 × 500 × 3.0 × 10−5 × π × (0.10)2 = 9.42 × 10−4 Wb. Average emf = 9.42 × 10−4/0.25 = 3.8 × 10−3 V, average current = 1.9 × 10−3 A.

A useful by-product: the charge that flows through a coil of resistance R when the flux linkage changes by ΔΦ is q = ΔΦ/R, independent of how fast the change happens. This is the principle of the ballistic galvanometer and of the search coil.

where: number of turns of the coil
rate of change of flux through one turn (Wb s<sup>−1</sup>)
charge that flows through the circuit (C)

sections.tip: If Φ is given as a polynomial in t, differentiate, then substitute the time. Students often substitute first and then get stuck. And remember the answer to 'average emf over a full rotation' is zero, however large the instantaneous values are.

sections.heading: 6.5 Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
sections.body:
Heinrich Lenz gave the rule for the sign in Faraday's law. The polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Note the wording: it opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself.

Apply it in two steps. First decide whether the flux through the loop is increasing or decreasing. Then choose the induced current so that its own field opposes that change: if the flux is increasing, the induced field points against the external field; if decreasing, it points along it. Two standard cases. The north pole of a magnet approaches a coil: flux increases, so the near face of the coil becomes a north pole to push the magnet away, and the current seen from the magnet is anticlockwise. The north pole is withdrawn: flux decreases, the near face becomes a south pole to pull the magnet back, and the current is clockwise as seen from the magnet.

Why Lenz's law is conservation of energy. Suppose the opposite were true and the near face became a south pole when the north pole approached. The magnet would be attracted, gain speed, cause a bigger induced current, be attracted more strongly, and so on, generating kinetic energy and electrical energy from nothing. That is impossible. In the real case, the magnet is repelled and you must do work to push it in; that work is exactly the energy dissipated as heat by the induced current. The direction given by Lenz's law is the only one consistent with conservation of energy.

Two consequences that appear as questions. A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls much more slowly than through a plastic tube, because the induced currents in the tube oppose its motion. A copper ring placed over the core of a solenoid jumps up when the current is switched on, because the sudden increase in flux induces a current whose field is opposite to the solenoid's, so the ring is repelled. The old NCERT section on eddy currents, now deleted, was built on the same law: currents induced in the body of a conductor oppose its motion, giving electromagnetic damping, magnetic braking and induction furnaces.

NCERT Exercise 6.2 uses the same reasoning with a change of area. If an irregularly shaped wire loop in a field pointing into the page is pulled into a circle, its area and hence its flux increase, so the induced current is anticlockwise (producing a field out of the page). If a circular loop is squeezed into a narrow straight line, its flux decreases, so the current is clockwise.
sections.tip: Never write 'the induced current opposes the flux'. Write 'opposes the change in flux'. Then name what changed (increasing or decreasing) before giving the direction.

sections.heading: 6.6 Motional Electromotive Force
sections.body:
Derivation from Faraday's law. A rectangular conductor PQRS lies in a uniform field B directed into the page. The arm PQ, of length l, is free to slide and is moved to the left with velocity v; RQ and SP are of length x at some instant. The flux through PQRS is ΦB = Blx. As PQ moves, x decreases, so

ε = −dΦB/dt = −Bl dx/dt = Blv

since dx/dt = −v. This emf is called the motional emf. If the circuit has resistance R the induced current is I = Blv/R.

Explanation by the Lorentz force. The rod PQ contains free electrons. Each electron, carried along with velocity v in a field B, experiences a force q(v × B) directed along the rod. The force does work qvBl in moving a charge from one end to the other, and emf is work per unit charge, so ε = Blv again. This is the argument to give when the question says 'explain using the Lorentz force' and it works even for an isolated rod with no closed circuit: charges pile up at the ends until the electric force balances the magnetic force, and a potential difference Blv appears across the rod.

If the rod moves at an angle θ to the field, only the perpendicular component counts, ε = Blv sin θ. A rod moving parallel to the field has no emf. NCERT Exercise 6.7 is a wire 10 m long, lying east-west, falling at 5.0 m s−1 through the horizontal component of the earth's field, 0.30 × 10−4 T. The emf is 0.30 × 10−4 × 10 × 5.0 = 1.5 × 10−3 V. With v downward and BH northward, v × B points east, so positive charge accumulates at the eastern end: the eastern end is at higher potential and the current in the wire, if the circuit were closed, would flow from west to east through it.

Rod rotating about one end. A metallic rod of length l rotates with angular speed ω about an axis through one end, perpendicular to a uniform field B. A small element of length dr at distance r from the axis moves with speed v = ωr, so it contributes dε = Bωr dr. Integrating from 0 to l: ε = Bω ∫ r dr = ½Bωl2. Equivalently, the rod sweeps area ½l2θ, so dΦ/dt = B · ½l2ω. NCERT Exercise 6.5: l = 1.0 m, ω = 400 rad s−1, B = 0.5 T gives ε = ½ × 0.5 × 400 × 1 = 100 V. For a wheel with many spokes, every spoke gives the same emf and they are in parallel, so the emf between axle and rim does not depend on the number of spokes.

Energy consideration. With the arm PQ carrying current I = Blv/R, the field exerts a force F = BIl = B2l2v/R on it, directed against its motion (Lenz's law). To keep the arm moving at constant v an external agent must push with this force, delivering power P = Fv = B2l2v2/R. The Joule heat in the circuit is I2R = (Blv/R)2 R = B2l2v2/R, the same. Mechanical work in equals electrical energy out.

where: uniform magnetic field, perpendicular to both l and v (T)
speed of the conductor perpendicular to B (m s<sup>−1</sup>)
angular speed of the rod about one end (rad s<sup>−1</sup>)
force needed to keep the arm moving at constant speed (N)

sections.tip: For the rotating rod, do not write ε = Blv with v = ωl; that gives twice the correct answer. The speed varies along the rod, so integrate, or use the average speed ½ωl.

sections.heading: 6.7 Inductance and 6.7.1 Mutual Inductance
sections.body:
An electric current produces a magnetic field, so the flux through a coil is proportional to the current that produces it, whether that current is in the coil itself or in a neighbouring coil. For a coil of N turns, the flux linkage NΦB ∝ I, and the constant of proportionality is called inductance. It depends only on the geometry of the coils and the medium, not on the current, just as capacitance depends on geometry and not on charge. Inductance is a scalar; its SI unit is the henry (H), and 1 H = 1 Wb A−1 = 1 V s A−1. Its dimensions are [M L2 T−2 A−2].

Mutual inductance is the flux linkage in one coil per unit current in a neighbouring coil: N1Φ1 = M12I2. Equivalently, it is the emf induced in one coil when the current in the other changes at 1 A s−1: ε1 = −M12 dI2/dt. The SI unit is the henry.

Derivation for two long coaxial solenoids (the standard 5-mark). Solenoid S1 of radius r1 and n1 turns per unit length sits inside solenoid S2 of radius r2 and n2 turns per unit length; both have length l. Pass current I2 through S2. The field inside it is B2 = μ0n2I2, and this field passes through all n1l turns of S1, each of area πr12. So N1Φ1 = (n1l)(μ0n2I2)(πr12) = M12I2, giving M12 = μ0n1n2πr12l. Now pass I1 through S1 instead. Its field μ0n1I1 exists only inside radius r1, so the flux through each turn of S2 is μ0n1I1πr12 (not πr22), and N2Φ2 = (n2l)(μ0n1I1)(πr12) = M21I1. Hence M21 = M12 = M = μ0n1n2πr12l. With a core of relative permeability μr, M = μrμ0n1n2πr12l.

M grows with the number of turns of each coil, with the area of the inner coil, and with a magnetic core; it falls when the coils are moved apart or their axes are turned away from each other, because less of one coil's flux threads the other. NCERT Example 6.7 does the same calculation for two concentric coplanar coils with r1 ≪ r2: the large coil's field at its centre, μ0I2/2r2, is nearly uniform over the small coil, so M = μ0πr12/2r2.

NCERT Exercise 6.9: M = 1.5 H and the current in one coil goes from 0 to 20 A in 0.5 s. Change in flux linkage with the other coil = MΔI = 1.5 × 20 = 30 Wb. The induced emf during the change is 30/0.5 = 60 V.

where: mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 (H)
flux linkage of coil 1 due to current I<sub>2</sub> in coil 2 (Wb)

formulas.expr: M = μ<sub>0</sub> n<sub>1</sub> n<sub>2</sub> π r<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> l
where: turns per unit length of the inner and outer solenoids

sections.tip: Use the inner radius r<sub>1</sub> in both halves of the derivation, and say why: the field of the inner solenoid is confined to its own cross-section. Marking schemes look for M<sub>12</sub> = M<sub>21</sub> as a stated conclusion.

sections.heading: 6.7.2 Self-Inductance
sections.body:
A changing current in a coil changes the flux through the coil itself, so an emf is induced in the same coil. This is self-induction. Self-inductance L is the flux linkage per unit current, NΦB = LI, or equivalently the emf induced in the coil when the current through it changes at 1 A s−1: ε = −L dI/dt. SI unit: henry. Its dimensional formula is [M L2 T−2 A−2].

Derivation for a long solenoid. Let the solenoid have n turns per unit length, cross-sectional area A and length l, carrying current I. The field inside is B = μ0nI. The total number of turns is N = nl, so the flux linkage is NΦB = (nl)(μ0nI)(A) = μ0n2AlI. Comparing with NΦB = LI, L = μ0n2Al. If the solenoid is filled with a material of relative permeability μr (a soft-iron core), L = μrμ0n2Al, which can be hundreds of times larger. Since n = N/l, the same result reads L = μ0N2A/l: doubling the turns in the same length gives four times the inductance.

Back emf and the inertia of electricity. By Lenz's law the self-induced emf opposes any change in current. When the current is switched on it opposes the growth; when the current is switched off it opposes the decay, which is why a large spark jumps at a switch that breaks a circuit containing a big inductor. Self-inductance plays the same role for current that mass plays for velocity, so it is called the electrical inertia of the circuit. NCERT Exercise 6.8: the current in a circuit falls from 5.0 A to 0 in 0.1 s and the average induced emf is 200 V, so L = ε/(dI/dt) = 200/(5.0/0.1) = 4 H.

Energy stored in an inductor. To build up a current against the back emf, the source must do work. At an instant when the current is I, the rate of work is |ε| I = LI dI/dt, so dW = LI dI. Integrating from 0 to I: W = ½LI2. This work is stored as magnetic energy U = ½LI2, in the field of the inductor, just as ½CV2 is stored in the electric field of a capacitor.

Substituting L = μ0n2Al and I = B/μ0n gives U = ½ μ0n2Al × B2/μ02n2 = B2Al/2μ0. Dividing by the volume Al, the magnetic energy density is u = B2/2μ0, which is the exact analogue of ½ε0E2 for an electric field.

Finally, when two coils are near each other and both currents change, the emf in coil 1 has both contributions: ε1 = −L1 dI1/dt − M12 dI2/dt.

where: rate of change of current in the coil (A s<sup>−1</sup>)

formulas.expr: L = μ<sub>0</sub> n<sup>2</sup> A l = μ<sub>0</sub> N<sup>2</sup> A / l
U = ½ L I<sup>2</sup>,  u = B<sup>2</sup>/2μ<sub>0</sub>
where: magnetic energy per unit volume (J m<sup>−3</sup>)

sections.tip: Self-inductance does not depend on the current. If a question says the current is doubled and asks what happens to L, the answer is 'nothing'; the flux linkage doubles, the stored energy quadruples.

sections.heading: 6.8 AC Generator
sections.body:
The AC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. Principle: when a coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field, the flux through it changes continuously and, by Faraday's law, an alternating emf is induced.

Construction. An armature, a coil of N turns and area A, is mounted on a shaft (the rotor) between the poles of a permanent magnet or an electromagnet (the field magnet). The two ends of the coil are joined to two slip rings that rotate with the shaft, and two stationary carbon brushes press against the rings to carry the current to the external circuit. The rotor is turned by a turbine driven by falling water (hydroelectric), by steam from burning coal (thermal) or from a nuclear reactor.

Derivation. Let the coil rotate with constant angular speed ω. At time t the angle between the field and the normal to the coil is θ = ωt (taking θ = 0 at t = 0). Flux through the coil: ΦB = BA cos ωt. By Faraday's law, for N turns,

ε = −N dΦB/dt = −NBA d(cos ωt)/dt = NBAω sin ωt

So ε = ε0 sin ωt with ε0 = NBAω, the maximum emf. Since ω = 2πν, ε = ε0 sin 2πνt, and ε0 = 2πνNBA. The emf is maximum when ωt = 90° or 270°, that is when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field: flux is zero there but changing fastest. It is zero when ωt = 0 or 180°, the plane of the coil perpendicular to the field, where flux is maximum but momentarily not changing. The graph of ε against t is a sine curve of period T = 1/ν; the emf changes sign every half rotation, which is why the output is alternating. Its average over a full cycle is zero.

In India the frequency is 50 Hz; in the USA it is 60 Hz. NCERT Example 6.8 (Kamla on the stationary bicycle): N = 100, A = 0.10 m2, B = 0.01 T, half a revolution per second, so ω = π rad s−1 and ε0 = 100 × 0.01 × 0.10 × π = 0.314 V. NCERT Exercise 6.6 asks for the same quantities with N = 20, r = 8.0 cm, ω = 50 rad s−1, B = 3.0 × 10−2 T and R = 10 Ω: ε0 = 20 × 0.03 × π(0.08)2 × 50 = 0.603 V, average emf over a cycle = 0, I0 = 0.0603 A, average power = ½ε0I0 = 0.018 W, and the power comes from the external agent that keeps the coil turning against the magnetic torque.

formulas.expr: ε = NBAω sin ωt = ε<sub>0</sub> sin ωt

sections.tip: Draw the diagram with the coil ABCD, the pole pieces N and S, the two slip rings and the two brushes labelled, and the external load. Marking schemes give a mark for the diagram and one for the graph; both are easy to lose by leaving out the labels.

key_terms.definition: The production of an emf (and hence a current in a closed circuit) whenever the magnetic flux linked with the circuit changes.
Φ<sub>B</sub> = B · A = BA cos θ, the number of field lines crossing a surface; a scalar measured in weber (Wb), where 1 Wb = 1 T m<sup>2</sup>.
For a coil of N turns each linking flux Φ<sub>B</sub>, the total flux linkage is NΦ<sub>B</sub>; it is proportional to the current producing it.
The magnitude of the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit: ε = −N dΦ<sub>B</sub>/dt.
The induced emf has a polarity that produces a current opposing the change in flux that caused it; it is a statement of conservation of energy.
The emf produced by a changing flux, and the current it drives in a closed circuit, I = ε/R. An emf exists even in an open circuit; a current needs a closed path.
The emf ε = Blv induced across a conductor of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a magnetic field B, due to the Lorentz force on its free charges.
The ratio of flux linkage to the current producing it, a property of the geometry of the coil and its surroundings; SI unit henry (H), 1 H = 1 Wb A<sup>−1</sup>.

Flux linkage produced in one coil per unit current in a neighbouring coil, N<sub>1</sub>Φ<sub>1</sub> = M I<sub>2</sub>; equivalently the emf induced in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other.
Flux linkage of a coil per unit current in the same coil, NΦ<sub>B</sub> = LI; the emf induced in a coil when its own current changes at 1 A s<sup>−1</sup>.
SI unit of inductance. A coil has inductance 1 H if a current changing at 1 A s<sup>−1</sup> induces an emf of 1 V in it.
The self-induced emf that opposes the change of current in an inductor, given by −L dI/dt; it is why self-inductance is called the electrical inertia of a circuit.
The work done against the back emf to establish a current I, stored in the magnetic field: U = ½LI<sup>2</sup>, with energy density B<sup>2</sup>/2μ<sub>0</sub>.
A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field, producing ε = NBAω sin ωt.

Two rings fixed to the rotating shaft, each connected to one end of the coil, with stationary carbon brushes pressing on them to carry the alternating current to the external circuit without twisting the wires.

Circulating currents induced in the body of a bulk conductor when the flux through it changes; they oppose the motion (Lenz's law). Deleted from the rationalised textbook but still a common context question.

ncert_questions.q: Predict the direction of induced current in the situations shown in NCERT Fig. 6.15 (a) to (f).
ncert_questions.a:
Use Lenz's law each time: find whether the flux through the loop is increasing or decreasing and pick the current whose field opposes that change.

  • (a) The S pole of the magnet moves towards the coil: flux increases, the near face must become S to repel the magnet, so the current is along qrpq (clockwise seen from the magnet).
  • (b) The magnets move away from both coils: flux decreases, the near faces attract the magnets, current along prq in the left coil and yzx in the right.
  • (c) The key is just closed, current in the left loop increasing, so the flux in the right loop increases: induced current along yzx.
  • (d) The rheostat setting is changed to reduce current: flux decreases, induced current along zyx.
  • (e) The key is released, the current in the left coil dies away, flux in the right coil decreases: induced current along xry.
  • (f) The wire lies in the plane of the loop, so no field line of the wire passes through the loop; the flux is always zero and no current is induced.

ncert_questions.q: Use Lenz's law to determine the direction of induced current when (a) a wire of irregular shape is turned into a circular loop, and (b) a circular loop is deformed into a narrow straight wire, both in a field directed into the plane of the paper.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) A circle encloses the largest area for a given perimeter, so the area and hence the flux (into the page) increase. The induced current must produce a field out of the page inside the loop: the current is anticlockwise, along adcba in the NCERT figure.

(b) When the circle is squeezed into a narrow line, the area and the flux decrease. The induced current must produce a field into the page: the current is clockwise, along a'd'c'b'a'.

ncert_questions.q: A long solenoid with 15 turns per cm has a small loop of area 2.0 cm<sup>2</sup> placed inside, normal to its axis. If the current in the solenoid changes steadily from 2.0 A to 4.0 A in 0.1 s, what is the induced emf in the loop while the current is changing?
ncert_questions.a:
n = 15 turns cm−1 = 1500 turns m−1; A = 2.0 × 10−4 m2; dI/dt = (4.0 − 2.0)/0.1 = 20 A s−1.

Field inside the solenoid B = μ0nI, so the flux through the loop is Φ = μ0nIA and

ε = dΦ/dt = μ0nA (dI/dt) = 4π × 10−7 × 1500 × 2.0 × 10−4 × 20 = 7.5 × 10−6 V.

ncert_questions.q: A rectangular wire loop of sides 8 cm and 2 cm with a small cut is moving out of a region of uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.3 T directed normal to the loop. What is the emf developed across the cut if the velocity of the loop is 1 cm s<sup>−1</sup> in a direction normal to the (a) longer side, (b) shorter side of the loop? For how long does the induced voltage last in each case?
ncert_questions.a:
ε = Blv, where l is the length of the side that cuts the field lines, and the emf lasts while the loop is leaving the field, that is for the time the other side takes to cross the boundary.

(a) Velocity normal to the longer side, so l = 8 cm = 0.08 m: ε = 0.3 × 0.08 × 0.01 = 2.4 × 10−4 V. Time = 2 cm ÷ 1 cm s−1 = 2 s.

(b) Velocity normal to the shorter side, so l = 2 cm = 0.02 m: ε = 0.3 × 0.02 × 0.01 = 0.6 × 10−4 V. Time = 8 cm ÷ 1 cm s−1 = 8 s.

ncert_questions.q: A 1.0 m long metallic rod is rotated with an angular frequency of 400 rad s<sup>−1</sup> about an axis normal to the rod passing through its one end. The other end of the rod is in contact with a circular metallic ring. A constant and uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T parallel to the axis exists everywhere. Calculate the emf developed between the centre and the ring.
ncert_questions.a:
For a rod rotating about one end, ε = ½Bωl2.

ε = ½ × 0.5 × 400 × (1.0)2 = 100 V.

Reason: an element dr at distance r moves with speed ωr and contributes dε = Bωr dr; integrating from 0 to l gives ½Bωl2.

ncert_questions.q: A circular coil of radius 8.0 cm and 20 turns is rotated about its vertical diameter with an angular speed of 50 rad s<sup>−1</sup> in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of magnitude 3.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup> T. Obtain the maximum and average emf induced in the coil. If the coil forms a closed loop of resistance 10 Ω, calculate the maximum value of current in the coil. Calculate the average power loss due to Joule heating. Where does this power come from?
ncert_questions.a:
A = π(0.08)2 = 2.01 × 10−2 m2. Flux Φ = NBA cos ωt, so ε = NBAω sin ωt.

Maximum emf ε0 = NBAω = 20 × 3.0 × 10−2 × 2.01 × 10−2 × 50 = 0.603 V.

Average emf over one full cycle = 0, because the emf is positive for half the cycle and negative for the other half.

Maximum current I0 = ε0/R = 0.603/10 = 0.0603 A.

Average power = ½ε0I0 = ½ × 0.603 × 0.0603 = 0.018 W.

The power comes from the external agent (rotor) that keeps the coil rotating against the torque exerted by the magnetic field on the induced current.

ncert_questions.q: A horizontal straight wire 10 m long extending from east to west is falling with a speed of 5.0 m s<sup>−1</sup> at right angles to the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field, 0.30 × 10<sup>−4</sup> Wb m<sup>−2</sup>. (a) What is the instantaneous value of the emf induced in the wire? (b) What is the direction of the emf? (c) Which end of the wire is at the higher electrical potential?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) ε = BHlv = 0.30 × 10−4 × 10 × 5.0 = 1.5 × 10−3 V.

(b) With v downward and BH pointing north, v × B points east, so the force on positive charge is eastward and the emf (and current, if the circuit were closed) is directed from west to east in the wire.

(c) Positive charge collects at the eastern end, so the eastern end is at the higher potential.

ncert_questions.q: Current in a circuit falls from 5.0 A to 0.0 A in 0.1 s. If an average emf of 200 V is induced, give an estimate of the self-inductance of the circuit.
A pair of adjacent coils has a mutual inductance of 1.5 H. If the current in one coil changes from 0 to 20 A in 0.5 s, what is the change of flux linkage with the other coil?
ncert_questions.a:
Flux linkage with the second coil is N2Φ2 = MI1, so the change is ΔΦ = M ΔI1 = 1.5 × 20 = 30 Wb.

(The emf induced in the second coil during the change is 30/0.5 = 60 V.)

ncert_questions.q: A jet plane is travelling towards west at a speed of 1800 km h<sup>−1</sup>. What is the voltage difference developed between the ends of the wing having a span of 25 m, if the earth's magnetic field at the location has a magnitude of 5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> T and the dip angle is 30°?
ncert_questions.a:
v = 1800 km h−1 = 1800 × 1000/3600 = 500 m s−1.

The wing and the velocity are both horizontal, so only the vertical component of the earth's field is cut: BV = B sin δ = 5 × 10−4 × sin 30° = 2.5 × 10−4 T.

ε = BVlv = 2.5 × 10−4 × 25 × 500 = 3.125 V ≈ 3.1 V.

The answer does not depend on the direction of flight, because the vertical field is perpendicular to every horizontal velocity.

ncert_questions.q: A square loop of side 10 cm and resistance 0.5 Ω is placed vertically in the east-west plane. A uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T is set up across the plane in the north-east direction. The field is decreased to zero in 0.70 s at a steady rate. Determine the magnitudes of induced emf and current during this interval.
ncert_questions.a:
The normal to a vertical east-west loop points north, so the field makes θ = 45° with the normal.

Initial flux Φ = BA cos 45° = 0.10 × (0.10)2 × 0.707 = 7.07 × 10−4 Wb; final flux = 0.

ε = ΔΦ/Δt = 7.07 × 10−4/0.70 = 1.0 × 10−3 V.

I = ε/R = 1.0 × 10−3/0.5 = 2.0 × 10−3 A.

ncert_questions.q: A wheel with 10 metallic spokes each 0.5 m long is rotated with a speed of 120 rev/min in a plane normal to the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field H<sub>E</sub> = 0.4 G. What is the induced emf between the axle and the rim of the wheel? (1 G = 10<sup>−4</sup> T.)
ncert_questions.a:
Each spoke is a rod rotating about one end: ε = ½Bωl2.

ω = 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s = 4π rad s−1; B = 0.4 × 10−4 T; l = 0.5 m.

ε = ½ × 0.4 × 10−4 × 4π × (0.5)2 = 6.28 × 10−5 V.

All ten spokes give the same emf and are connected in parallel between axle and rim, so the number of spokes makes no difference to the emf.

ncert_questions.q: Two concentric circular coils, one of small radius r<sub>1</sub> and the other of large radius r<sub>2</sub>, such that r<sub>1</sub> ≪ r<sub>2</sub>, are placed coaxially with centres coinciding. Obtain the mutual inductance of the arrangement.
ncert_questions.a:
Let current I2 flow in the large coil. The field at its centre is B2 = μ0I2/2r2. Since r1 ≪ r2, this field is nearly uniform over the whole area of the small coil, so the flux through it is

Φ1 = πr12 × μ0I2/2r2 = M12I2

Hence M12 = M21 = M = μ0πr12/2r2.

Calculating M21 directly (small coil carrying current, flux through the large coil) would be hard because that field is non-uniform; the equality M12 = M21 lets us pick the easy route.

pyq.q: The magnetic flux linked with a coil is given by Φ = 5t<sup>2</sup> + 3t + 16, where Φ is in weber and t in seconds. The magnitude of the induced emf at t = 4 s is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: ε = dΦ/dt = 10t + 3. At t = 4 s, ε = 40 + 3 = 43 V. Differentiate first, then substitute.

pyq.q: A metal rod moves with velocity v parallel to a uniform magnetic field B. The emf induced across its ends is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The Lorentz force q(v × B) is zero when v is parallel to B, so no charge separation occurs and the emf is zero.

pyq.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: If the induced current did not oppose the change in flux, a magnet would accelerate into a coil while producing electrical energy, creating energy from nothing.

pyq.q: The self-inductance of a long air-cored solenoid becomes double when
options: the current through it is doubled
its length is doubled keeping the number of turns per unit length the same
the number of turns per unit length is doubled keeping the length the same
its area of cross-section is halved
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: L = μ<sub>0</sub>n<sup>2</sup>Al. Doubling l at fixed n doubles L; doubling n gives 4L; halving A halves L; current does not enter.

pyq.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards a circular coil. As seen from the magnet, the induced current in the coil is
options: zero, since the magnet is not inside the coil
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The flux increases, so the near face must become a north pole to repel the magnet. A face is a north pole when the current in it is anticlockwise as seen by the observer.

pyq.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.005 H. The current in the first coil is I = I<sub>0</sub> sin ωt with I<sub>0</sub> = 10 A and ω = 100π rad s<sup>−1</sup>. The maximum emf induced in the second coil is
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: ε = M dI/dt = M I<sub>0</sub> ω cos ωt, so ε<sub>max</sub> = M I<sub>0</sub> ω = 0.005 × 10 × 100π = 5π V ≈ 15.7 V.

pyq.q: In an AC generator the induced emf is maximum when the plane of the armature coil is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: ε = NBAω sin ωt is maximum at ωt = 90°, when the normal is perpendicular to B, that is the plane of the coil is parallel to B. The flux is zero there but changing fastest.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): No emf is induced in a rod moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field. Reason (R): Motional emf depends only on the component of the velocity perpendicular to the magnetic field.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: ε = Blv sin θ. With v parallel to B the perpendicular component is zero, so the emf is zero; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Self-inductance is called the inertia of electricity. Reason (R): The self-induced emf in a coil always opposes any change in the current flowing through it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Just as inertia opposes a change in velocity, self-inductance opposes a change in current through the back emf −L dI/dt. R is exactly why A is said.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The self-inductance of a coil increases when the current through it is increased. Reason (R): Self-inductance is defined as the flux linkage per unit current, L = NΦ<sub>B</sub>/I.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The flux linkage grows in proportion to the current, so their ratio L stays fixed; L depends on the geometry, turns and core only. A is false, R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A copper ring placed loosely over the vertical core of a solenoid jumps up when the current in the solenoid is switched on. Reason (R): Copper is a good conductor of electricity.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The ring jumps because the sudden rise in flux induces a current whose field opposes the solenoid's field (Lenz's law), so the ring is repelled. Copper's conductivity allows a large induced current but is not the reason for the repulsion.

pyq.q: State Lenz's law. Show that it is consistent with the law of conservation of energy.
pyq.answer:
Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

Consistency with energy conservation: when the north pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil, the near face becomes a north pole and repels the magnet. Work must be done against this repulsion, and this work appears as the electrical energy of the induced current. If instead the near face became a south pole, the magnet would be pulled in with increasing speed, producing electrical energy and kinetic energy without any work being done, which violates conservation of energy. So the direction given by Lenz's law is the only one allowed.

pyq.q: Define self-inductance of a coil. Write its SI unit and state the factors on which it depends.
pyq.answer:
The self-inductance of a coil is the magnetic flux linked with the coil per unit current flowing through it, L = NΦB/I; equivalently, it is the emf induced in the coil when the current through it changes at the rate of 1 A s−1.

SI unit: henry (H). 1 H = 1 Wb A−1 = 1 V s A−1.

It depends on the number of turns (L ∝ N2), the area of cross-section, the length of the coil, and the permeability of the core material. It does not depend on the current.

pyq.q: How does the mutual inductance of a pair of coils change when (i) the distance between the coils is increased, and (ii) the number of turns in each coil is decreased? Give reasons.
pyq.answer:
(i) It decreases. With greater separation a smaller fraction of the flux produced by one coil passes through the other, so the flux linkage per unit current falls.

(ii) It decreases. For coaxial solenoids M = μ0n1n2πr12l, so M is proportional to the product of the numbers of turns; fewer turns in each coil means a smaller field from the first coil and fewer turns of the second to link it.

pyq.q: A long straight current-carrying wire passes normally through the centre of a circular loop. If the current in the wire increases, will there be an induced emf in the loop? Justify.
pyq.answer: No. The magnetic field lines of a straight wire are concentric circles around the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to it. The loop lies in such a plane, so the field lines run along the loop and none of them cross its surface. The flux through the loop is zero at all times, however the current changes, so dΦ/dt = 0 and no emf is induced.

pyq.q: The graph of flux linkage (NΦ) against current I is drawn for two inductors A and B on the same axes. The line for A is steeper than the line for B. Which inductor has the larger self-inductance? A current of 2 A is switched off in 0.1 s in inductor A whose inductance is 0.5 H; find the average induced emf.
pyq.answer:
NΦ = LI, so the slope of the NΦ–I line equals L. The steeper line belongs to the larger self-inductance: A has the larger self-inductance.

|ε| = L ΔI/Δt = 0.5 × 2/0.1 = 10 V.

pyq.q: A metallic rod of length l is rotated with angular speed ω about an axis passing through one of its ends and perpendicular to its length, in a uniform magnetic field B directed parallel to the axis. Derive the expression for the emf induced between the ends of the rod. Explain using the Lorentz force why an emf appears.
pyq.answer:
Why an emf appears: every free electron in the rod moves in a circle with the rod. In the field B it experiences a Lorentz force −e(v × B) directed along the rod, which pushes electrons towards one end. Charge separates until the electric force balances the magnetic force, leaving a potential difference between the ends.

Derivation: consider an element of length dr at a distance r from the axis. Its linear speed is v = ωr, so the motional emf across it is dε = Bv dr = Bωr dr.

Emf across the whole rod: ε = ∫0l Bωr dr = Bω [r2/2]0l = ½Bωl2.

Alternatively, in time dt the rod sweeps an area ½l2 dθ, so dΦ/dt = B · ½l2 ω, giving the same result. If ν is the frequency of rotation, ε = πBνl2.

pyq.q: A conducting rod PQ of length 20 cm slides on two parallel metal rails at a constant speed of 5 m s<sup>−1</sup>. A uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T acts perpendicular to the plane of the rails, and the resistance of the closed circuit is 2 Ω. Find (i) the emf induced across PQ, (ii) the current in the circuit, (iii) the force required to keep the rod moving, and (iv) the power delivered by this force. Compare (iv) with the rate of Joule heating.
pyq.answer:
(i) ε = Blv = 0.4 × 0.20 × 5 = 0.4 V.

(ii) I = ε/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A.

(iii) The field exerts a force BIl on the current-carrying rod, opposing its motion (Lenz's law). To keep the speed constant an equal external force is needed: F = BIl = 0.4 × 0.2 × 0.20 = 0.016 N.

(iv) P = Fv = 0.016 × 5 = 0.08 W.

Rate of Joule heating = I2R = (0.2)2 × 2 = 0.08 W. The two are equal: all the mechanical work done on the rod is converted into heat in the circuit.

pyq.q: Define self-inductance of a coil. Obtain the expression for the magnetic energy stored in an inductor of self-inductance L when a current I is built up in it.
pyq.answer:
Self-inductance is the flux linkage of a coil per unit current flowing in it, L = NΦB/I, or the emf induced in the coil per unit rate of change of its own current. SI unit: henry.

Energy stored: as the current in the inductor grows, a back emf ε = −L dI/dt opposes the growth. To push charge through against this emf, the source does work at the rate

dW/dt = |ε| I = L I (dI/dt), so dW = L I dI.

Total work done while the current rises from 0 to I:

W = ∫0I L I dI = ½ L I2.

This work is stored as magnetic potential energy in the inductor: U = ½LI2. It is released when the current is switched off, which is what produces the spark at the switch.

pyq.q: A rectangular loop and a circular loop are moving out of a region of uniform magnetic field with the same constant velocity, the field being perpendicular to their planes. In which loop is the induced emf constant during its passage out of the field? Explain.
pyq.answer:
The induced emf is ε = −dΦ/dt = −B dA/dt, where A is the area still inside the field.

For the rectangular loop, with one side of length l perpendicular to the velocity, the area inside the field decreases at the constant rate dA/dt = lv. So ε = Blv is constant throughout the time the loop is leaving the field.

For the circular loop, the length of the chord that is crossing the field boundary changes continuously: it is small at first, grows to the diameter, and shrinks again. So dA/dt, and hence the emf, keeps changing. The rectangular loop is the one with a constant induced emf.

pyq.q: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm has a resistance of 5 Ω. It is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T, which is reduced to zero uniformly in 0.1 s. Find the induced emf, the induced current and the total charge that flows through the coil.
pyq.answer:
A = π(0.10)2 = 3.14 × 10−2 m2.

Change in flux linkage: NΔΦ = NBA = 100 × 0.2 × 3.14 × 10−2 = 0.628 Wb.

Emf: ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 0.628/0.1 = 6.28 V.

Current: I = ε/R = 6.28/5 = 1.26 A.

Charge: q = IΔt = 1.26 × 0.1 = 0.126 C, or directly q = NΔΦ/R = 0.628/5 = 0.126 C. The charge does not depend on how fast the field is switched off.

pyq.q: (a) Define mutual inductance and write its SI unit. (b) Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length wound one over the other. (c) A coil of mutual inductance 0.2 H with respect to another coil has the current in the other coil changed from 2 A to 8 A in 0.3 s. Find the emf induced in the first coil.
pyq.answer:
(a) The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the magnetic flux linked with one coil per unit current flowing in the other, N1Φ1 = M I2. Equivalently it is the emf induced in one coil when the current in the other changes at 1 A s−1. SI unit: henry (H).

(b) Let solenoid S1 (radius r1, n1 turns per unit length) lie inside solenoid S2 (radius r2, n2 turns per unit length), both of length l, on a common axis.

Pass current I2 through S2. The field inside is B2 = μ0n2I2. It links all N1 = n1l turns of S1, each of area πr12:

N1Φ1 = n1l × μ0n2I2 × πr12 = M12I2, so M12 = μ0n1n2πr12l.

Now pass I1 through S1. Its field μ0n1I1 is confined to its own cross-section πr12, so the flux through each turn of S2 is μ0n1I1πr12, and

N2Φ2 = n2l × μ0n1I1 × πr12 = M21I1, so M21 = μ0n1n2πr12l.

Hence M12 = M21 = M = μ0n1n2πr12l. With a core of relative permeability μr, M = μrμ0n1n2πr12l.

(c) |ε| = M ΔI/Δt = 0.2 × (8 − 2)/0.3 = 0.2 × 20 = 4 V.

pyq.q: (a) Derive the expression for the motional emf induced in a conductor of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, using Faraday's law. (b) Explain the origin of this emf using the Lorentz force on the charge carriers. (c) If the conductor forms part of a closed circuit of resistance R, show that the power supplied by the external agent moving the conductor equals the rate of Joule heating.
pyq.answer:
(a) Take a rectangular conductor PQRS in a uniform field B into the page, with the arm PQ of length l sliding to the left at speed v, and let x be the length of the loop inside the field. The flux through PQRS is ΦB = Blx. By Faraday's law,

ε = −dΦB/dt = −Bl (dx/dt) = Blv, since dx/dt = −v.

(b) The rod carries free electrons that move with it at velocity v. Each experiences the Lorentz force q(v × B) = qvB along the rod, so electrons are pushed to one end. The work done by this force in carrying a charge q along the full length l is qvBl. Emf is the work done per unit charge, ε = qvBl/q = Blv. This shows the emf exists even without a closed circuit; it appears as a potential difference between the ends of the rod.

(c) With the circuit closed, I = Blv/R. The field exerts a force on the current-carrying arm, F = BIl = B2l2v/R, directed opposite to v by Lenz's law. To keep the arm moving at constant speed the external agent must apply an equal force, delivering power

P = Fv = B2l2v2/R.

Rate of Joule heating = I2R = (Blv/R)2R = B2l2v2/R.

They are equal, so the mechanical energy supplied is entirely converted to electrical energy and then to heat. This is conservation of energy, and Lenz's law is what makes the force oppose the motion.

pyq.q: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram, the principle and working of an AC generator. (b) Derive an expression for the instantaneous emf induced in the coil and draw the graph showing its variation with time. (c) A coil of 100 turns and area 0.1 m<sup>2</sup> rotates at 50 rev s<sup>−1</sup> in a field of 0.1 T. Find the peak emf.
pyq.answer:
(a) Principle: when a coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field, the flux linked with it changes continuously, so by Faraday's law an emf is induced; the emf reverses every half rotation, giving alternating current.

Construction: an armature coil ABCD of N turns and area A on a shaft between the poles N and S of a field magnet; the coil's ends are connected to two slip rings R1, R2 that rotate with it; two fixed carbon brushes B1, B2 press on the rings and connect to the external load. The shaft is turned by a turbine (water, steam or nuclear).

Working: as the coil turns, the arms AB and CD cut the field lines in opposite senses, so the emfs in them add around the loop. After half a rotation each arm moves the other way and the emf reverses. The slip rings carry this alternating emf to the load.

(b) At time t the angle between B and the normal to the coil is ωt, so ΦB = NBA cos ωt.

ε = −dΦB/dt = −NBA (−ω sin ωt) = NBAω sin ωt = ε0 sin ωt, where ε0 = NBAω.

Graph: a sine curve of ε against t with amplitude ε0 and period T = 2π/ω; ε = 0 at t = 0, T/2, T (coil perpendicular to B) and ε = ±ε0 at t = T/4, 3T/4 (coil parallel to B).

(c) ω = 2πν = 2π × 50 = 100π rad s−1. ε0 = NBAω = 100 × 0.1 × 0.1 × 100π = 100π = 314 V.

pyq.q: (a) Define self-inductance and give its SI unit. (b) Derive the expression for the self-inductance of a long air-cored solenoid of length l, cross-sectional area A and n turns per unit length. (c) How does the self-inductance change when a soft-iron core is inserted? (d) Show that the magnetic energy density in the solenoid is B<sup>2</sup>/2μ<sub>0</sub>.
pyq.answer:
(a) Self-inductance is the flux linkage of a coil per unit current flowing through it, NΦB = LI; equivalently the emf induced in the coil when the current changes at 1 A s−1, ε = −L dI/dt. SI unit: henry.

(b) For a long solenoid carrying current I, the field inside is B = μ0nI. Total turns N = nl. Flux through each turn ΦB = BA = μ0nIA.

Flux linkage NΦB = nl × μ0nIA = μ0n2AlI.

Comparing with NΦB = LI: L = μ0n2Al.

(c) With a core of relative permeability μr, the field becomes μrμ0nI, so L = μrμ0n2Al. Soft iron has μr of the order of a thousand, so L increases by that factor.

(d) Energy stored U = ½LI2. Put L = μ0n2Al and I = B/μ0n:

U = ½ μ0n2Al × B2/(μ02n2) = B2Al/2μ0.

The volume of the solenoid is Al, so the energy per unit volume is u = B2/2μ0, the magnetic analogue of ½ε0E2.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student drops a small strong magnet through a vertical copper tube and then through an identical plastic tube. The magnet takes noticeably longer to fall through the copper tube, even though copper is not magnetic. As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring-shaped slice of the tube below it increases and the flux through each slice above it decreases. Currents are induced in the tube wall, and by Lenz's law their fields oppose the motion of the magnet. The tube also becomes slightly warm.
(i) Why does the magnet fall slowly in the copper tube but not in the plastic tube?
(ii) State the law that fixes the direction of the induced currents.
(iii) Where does the kinetic energy that the magnet fails to gain go?
(iv) If the copper tube were cut along its length so that it no longer forms closed rings, how would the fall time change, and why?
pyq.answer:
(i) The changing flux induces currents in the copper wall which, by Lenz's law, produce fields that oppose the magnet's motion, so it is retarded. Plastic is an insulator; no current can flow, so there is no opposing force and the magnet falls freely.

(ii) Lenz's law: the induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux producing it.

(iii) It is converted into electrical energy of the induced currents and then into heat in the tube wall (I2R heating), which is why the tube warms; total energy is conserved.

(iv) The fall time would decrease, approaching that in the plastic tube, because the currents need closed circular paths around the tube. Cutting the tube along its length breaks these paths, so the induced currents and the retarding force become much smaller.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. In an AC generator a coil of N turns and area A rotates with angular speed ω in a uniform magnetic field B. The flux through the coil at time t is Φ = NBA cos ωt and the induced emf is ε = NBAω sin ωt. Slip rings and brushes carry the emf to the external circuit. In India the generated frequency is 50 Hz.
(i) At what orientation of the coil is the induced emf zero? Is the flux zero or maximum then?
(ii) Write the expression for the peak emf and state two ways of doubling it.
(iii) What is the role of the slip rings?
(iv) A generator coil of 200 turns and area 0.05 m2 rotates at 50 rev s−1 in a field of 0.2 T. Find the peak emf.
pyq.answer:
(i) The emf is zero when sin ωt = 0, that is when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. At that instant the flux is maximum (NBA), but its rate of change is zero.

(ii) ε0 = NBAω = 2πνNBA. It can be doubled by doubling the number of turns, the area, the field, or the speed of rotation (any one of them).

(iii) The slip rings rotate with the coil and each stays permanently connected to one end of it; the stationary brushes press on them, so the alternating emf reaches the external circuit without the connecting wires twisting.

(iv) ω = 2π × 50 = 100π rad s−1. ε0 = 200 × 0.2 × 0.05 × 100π = 2 × 100π = 200π ≈ 628 V.

common_mistakes: Writing Lenz's law as 'the induced current opposes the flux'. It opposes the change in flux. Examiners deduct for the missing word, and the wrong wording leads to the wrong direction when the flux is decreasing.
Using v = ωl in ε = Blv for a rotating rod, which gives Bωl<sup>2</sup>, twice the correct ½Bωl<sup>2</sup>. The speed varies along the rod; integrate or use the average speed.
Taking θ in Φ = BA cos θ from the plane of the coil instead of from the normal. A field 'in the plane of the coil' gives zero flux, not maximum.

Using the outer radius r<sub>2</sub> in the mutual inductance of coaxial solenoids. The field of the inner solenoid exists only within r<sub>1</sub>, so πr<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> appears in both M<sub>12</sub> and M<sub>21</sub>.
Saying that self-inductance increases with current. L = NΦ/I is a constant of the coil; only the flux linkage and stored energy change with current.
Forgetting the factor N when a coil has many turns, or applying it twice: ε = N dΦ/dt where Φ is the flux through one turn.
Reporting the average emf of a rotating coil as NBAω. Over a full cycle the average is zero; NBAω is the peak.

Forgetting to convert units: turns per cm to turns per m, cm<sup>2</sup> to m<sup>2</sup>, km h<sup>−1</sup> to m s<sup>−1</sup>, rev/min to rad s<sup>−1</sup>. The jet-plane and spoked-wheel problems are lost almost entirely to this.
strategy:
This is a small chapter with a short list of fixed derivations, so it rewards a disciplined two-day plan. On day one, learn the five derivations until you can write each from memory in under five minutes: motional emf ε = Blv from Faraday's law and from the Lorentz force; the rotating rod ε = ½Bωl2; mutual inductance of coaxial solenoids M = μ0n1n2πr12l; self-inductance of a solenoid L = μ0n2Al with the energy ½LI2 and density B2/2μ0; and the AC generator ε = NBAω sin ωt with its diagram and graph. Every one of them starts with ε = −dΦ/dt and a clear statement of what Φ is, so write that line first each time.

On day two, do the numericals. Work all ten NCERT exercises and Examples 6.2, 6.3, 6.6 and 6.7 with your own hand; the board lifts questions from them almost unchanged. Then practise the Lenz's law direction questions until the two-step method (is the flux increasing or decreasing; which current opposes that) is automatic, because they appear as 1- and 2-mark questions every year and are quick marks.

Memorise the definitions of magnetic flux, self-inductance and mutual inductance with their units in NCERT wording, and the statement of Lenz's law with the words 'change in flux'. Know that eddy currents and the quantitative energy treatment were removed from the rationalised textbook, but keep the energy argument for the moving arm ready as it is a natural 3-mark question. In the paper, budget about 8 minutes for a 5-mark derivation, including the diagram, and check units before writing any final number.
